props.title: 50 First Dates
props.initialSlug: Falling in love, one day at a time.

sections.content: 50 First Dates reinvents the romantic comedy formula by infusing it with a bittersweet medical premise reminiscent of Memento (2000). Adam Sandler and Drew Barrymore's second pairing after The Wedding Singer (1998) tackles short-term memory loss with surprising depth, while maintaining their signature chemistry. The Hawaiian setting provides more than just scenic backdrops - it creates a contained world where Lucy's (Barrymore) daily reset feels both tragic and manageable. The film cleverly uses humor to explore serious questions about love's persistence and identity.

sections.content: Memory-based romance films gained significant traction in the early 2000s, with Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind (2004) releasing the same year as 50 First Dates. While both films deal with memory loss, they approach it from opposite directions - one voluntary erasure, the other involuntary retention. This theme continues in films like Before We Go (2014) and The Lake House (2006), where time and memory become obstacles for lovers to overcome.

The film's handling of disability stands out among Adam Sandler's comedies. Unlike the broad humor of Billy Madison (1995) or Happy Gilmore (1996), 50 First Dates treats Lucy's condition with respect while finding humor in the situations rather than the disability itself. This approach influenced later films like Silver Linings Playbook (2012) and The Big Sick (2017), where medical conditions become part of the narrative without defining it entirely. sections.content: The success of 50 First Dates helped pave the way for more complex romantic comedies that weren't afraid to tackle serious subjects. Films like Me Before You (2016) and Everything, Everything (2017) followed this template of combining romance with medical challenges. The film's ending - showing Henry's daily video routine and their life together - offers a more nuanced resolution than typical rom-com fare, acknowledging both the permanence of Lucy's condition and the depth of their commitment.
